BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The pattern through the extended will feature a broad upper level ridge extending across the central CONUS while a deep trough becomes established off the Pacific Northwest coast.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to slightly above normal temperatures through the week.
- Scattered showers across the north on Thursday.
- Above normal temperatures and dry over the weekend into early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The pattern will remain progressive during the short term but overall remain quiet. An upper low over northern Nevada early this morning will move east today as a shortwave ridge builds overhead. Skies will clear this morning with lighter winds and highs near to slightly above normal. Clouds will increase tonight ahead of a weak upper level trough moving through on Thursday. A 10-30% chance of showers will develop across the north with minimal precipitation amounts expected. A dusting of snow is possible above 4500-6000 feet. This system will cool temperatures a few degrees and bring an uptick in wind Thursday afternoon. A ridge of high pressure will build on Friday bringing slight warming and periods of high clouds. Otherwise, winds will be light with no precipitation expected. Patchy fog will develop each night this week in sheltered basins.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The pattern through the extended will feature a broad upper level ridge extending across the central CONUS while a deep trough becomes established off the Pacific Northwest coast. The ridge and southwesterly flow aloft through the period will push temperatures to around 10 degrees above normal, with valley highs generally reaching the 60s. Breezy southeast winds will develop over the weekend as a system clips the Pacific Northwest. However, precipitation will remain north of our area with only periods of high clouds. Dry conditions will persist into early next week, but a 10-30% chance of precipitation and breezy conditions will return on Wednesday as a strong system approaches the coast.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: There is still good agreement that ridging aloft moves back in for Thursday followed by a trough passing to our north on Friday. This system will lack moisture for our area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Precipitation will form across the mountains and foothills along and south of I-70 for this afternoon through early Thursday morning.
- Snowfall amounts of 3-10" with isolated higher amounts possible.
- The highest snowfall amounts and worst road conditions are expected for western Park County, possibly extending into northern Park County.
- Pleasant temperatures and dry conditions are expected Thursday through early next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: We are expecting a quiet overnight with mostly clear skies. Skies will be partly cloudy in the morning with increasing clouds by Wednesday afternoon for the high country, Denver metro, and the adjacent plains. Temperatures will top out in the mid to upper 50s for the plains once again. The trough and associated low are currently over Nevada. As this feature moves east, it will bring us the 2nd storm system of the week, which will quickly move through our area on Wednesday afternoon and into Wednesday night. We expect the highest impacts for the central and southern high country.

Precipitation will increase from west to east starting mid afternoon on Wednesday in the high country. The precipitation shield should shift south and east through Wednesday evening and into the overnight. On Wednesday evening, scattered rain showers and perhaps a few snowflakes mixing in are possible for the Palmer Divide. There is a low but nonzero chance (~10-15%) that this potential could even extend into far southern and western parts of the Denver metro. No snow accumulation is expected in these locations. Some rain showers are possible for southern Lincoln County late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning as the low pushes off to the east of our area.

High resolution model guidance has shown an uptick in moisture compared to model runs over the last 24-36 hours. As the afternoon progresses on Wednesday, there should be some modest instability present in the southern high country along with increasing lapse rates. Snow levels are trending lower as well. Snow levels should start around 9,000 feet early Wednesday afternoon. They are now forecast to drop down to 7,500-8,000 feet on Wednesday evening. Snow levels should drop even lower to 6,500-7,000 feet just as the system starts to exit the area early Thursday AM. The track of the low across our southwestern counties or just to the south would bring northeast to east winds at the surface. This flow could extend up in the atmosphere a few kilometers. In this type of flow, Park County looks favored for some upslope flow/enhancement. In particular, the southern Front Range foothills, the Mosquito Range, the Highway 285 corridor, and most of Park County look favored for the heaviest snowfall totals from this system.

Altogether, most short-term models have trended up with snowfall totals and QPF in the last 24-36 hours. QPF amounts of 0.25-0.75" should be common in Park County and adjacent locations with isolated higher amounts possible at the highest elevations. DESI probabilities are honing in on the Mosquito Range/western Park County where there is a 50-60% chance that these locations receive 6 inches or more of snowfall. Thus, we have issued a Winter Weather Advisory for the mountains of Summit County, Park County, the Mosquito Range, Indian Peaks, and South Park. It runs from 2pm Wednesday to 2am Thursday. Most of Park County should get 3+ inches snowfall with the Mosquito Range forecast to receive 5-10 inches of snowfall with localized higher amounts possible. Areas along and adjacent to the I-70 corridor above 7,500 feet, including the northern Gore Range, are forecast to get 3-6 inches of snowfall with areas to the north getting much less.

There is still good agreement that ridging aloft moves back in for Thursday followed by a trough passing to our north on Friday. This system will lack moisture for our area. As a result, there are only low precipitation chances for Friday afternoon in the high country. Temperatures are forecast to reach the mid to upper 50s for the plains on Thursday and Friday. Ridging resumes once again for the weekend and into next week. We expect dry conditions across our area from Saturday through the end of the forecast period. The ridge is expected to strengthen and the center should move closer to us for the end of the weekend and into early next week. Mid 60s look increasingly likely for Denver for Sunday and Monday according to ensemble guidance. This would be 5-10 degrees above average for this time of year. Temperatures on the eastern plains could even be pushing 70 F. For Tuesday, more zonal flow could be in place dropping high temperatures back into the low 60s for most of the plains.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Once that system moves through the area, models are in fairly good agreement showing clean ridging building back into the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near average temperatures and mostly dry conditions are expected through the rest of the work week.
- Warmer temperatures are expected to return this weekend with largely dry weather continuing.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Mostly clear skies and light winds early this morning are helping to get our Wednesday off to a chilly start, with most locations below freezing. We still have some lingering humidity after Monday's storm system, which is leading to patchy fog formation, mainly in valleys west of the Laramie Range. This is not expected to be as consistent as the fog we saw last week, but don't be surprised to see some localized visibility reductions heading out this morning. While the area is largely clear now, cloud cover is expected to increase shortly as a compact upper level low cutting underneath the upper level ridge approaches the area. While most lift and moisture associated with this system, we may see some light showers / high elevation snow showers developing primarily in Carbon county as the system slides to our south today. The cloud shield may not cover the entire area, but expect those southwest of a roughly Douglas to Sidney line to be fairly cloudy today. Temperatures will be held slightly below seasonal norms as a result. Winds are expected to be light today.

On Thursday, our area will be in between successive weak upper level lows traveling underneath the messy ridge aloft. Look for more sunshine for much of the day, and temperatures a few degrees warmer than Wednesday (and near average). Ridging won't have much time to recover in between systems, so spiking temperatures are not expected this time. Cloud cover will start to increase Thursday evening in advance of the next upper level low / vort-max.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The next upper level low will traverse across the region in the Friday or Friday night time period, but models are all over the place concerning what to do with this system. However, all scenarios are fairly low impact regardless of the exact track of the upper level low, which differs from just north of our area all the way to northern Mexico. About 25% of ensemble members (mostly from the GEFS) move the compact upper level low through our area, which would bring the potential for some light precipitation on Friday. Low end PoPs (15 to 20%) were introduced with this update to account for this possibility. With this bit of unsettled weather around, temperatures should remain fairly close to or slightly above seasonal averages Friday and Saturday.

Once that system moves through the area, models are in fairly good agreement showing clean ridging building back into the area. NAEFS mean 700-mb temperatures climb to the +6 to +8C range over much of the area by Sunday, above the climatological 90th percentile. Temperatures are expected to surge well above normal for Sunday, and remain there into the early part of next week. Look for highs generally in the 60s east of the Laramie range, and mid to upper 50s to the west. These values are about 10F above average. Precipitation chances look to remain minimal during this period. There is a slim chances (about 25%) for some elevated winds Sunday night or Monday as the ridge flattens out and the jet stream gets slightly closer to the area.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Beyond Thursday morning, the forecast overall looks to trend much drier. A quick moving shortwave skirts the region across the north on Friday which could bring some increased clouds and isolated showers over the Divide with little impact.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rivers and other waterways across southwest Colorado and southeast Utah remain elevated due to runoff. A few Flood Warnings remain in effect for those impacted areas.

- A quick-hitting round of valley rain and mountain snow moves through along the I-70 and central mountain corridor Wednesday afternoon through Wednesday night/Thursday morning. 4 to 8 inches of snow is expected above 10,000 feet across the central mountain corridor and Elk Mountains where a Winter Weather Advisory has been issued. Slick travel is expected to develop over mountain passes.
- Warmer and drier conditions highlight the remainder of the seven-day forecast.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A low pressure system currently over northern California will move across the Great Basin and move across the central portions of our CWA, mainly impacting the central mountain corridor Wednesday afternoon through Wednesday night/Thursday morning. This is a quick hitter of a system but looks to pack a punch as some colder air arrives with it as H7 temps drop to -3 to -8C range Wednesday evening. This will bring valley rain and mountain snow with elevations above 10,000 feet favored for 4 to 8 inches across the I-70 and central mountain corridor including the Elk Mountains. Decided to issue a Winter Weather Advisory for COZ010 above 10,000 feet from 2 pm MST Wednesday through 5 am MST Thursday as roadways and passes above 10,000 feet are expected to become slick and slushy impacting travel for the Wednesday evening and Thursday morning commute. Slow down and be prepared for winter driving conditions if you are out as road conditions could change rapidly as this system moves through.

There is some uncertainty though for convective potential which could lead to heavier rain/snow rates, increasing potential impacts. Localized flash flooding is possible if stronger rain showers/storms develop over saturated or flood-prone areas, and hazardous travel conditions could develop over areas that see convective bursts of snow even outside of the current Winter Weather Advisory.

Beyond Thursday morning, the forecast overall looks to trend much drier. A quick moving shortwave skirts the region across the north on Friday which could bring some increased clouds and isolated showers over the Divide with little impact. A broad ridge of high pressure moves in late this week into the coming weekend, with temperatures warming to above seasonable levels and providing a much needed break from the recent wet weather.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Sunday - Tuesday: For the end of the weekend and into early next week. Quiet weather makes a return to south central and southeastern Colorado. Overall, ridging is expected to make a return, bringing increased subsidence and drier air to the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow showers expected across the mountains today and tonight, which could bring slick and hazardous travel.
- Drier and warmer conditions return early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today - Tomorrow Night: For midweek week, a brief period of active weather is anticipated for south central and southeastern Colorado. A compact and quick moving wave will pass over the area through Wednesday into early Thursday, bringing increased forcing and support, along with stronger orographic forcing as flow increases. These forcing mechanisms, along with modest moisture in place, will allow for scattered to widespread showers to develop across the region, blooming from the northwest along the higher terrain Wednesday afternoon, and to the southeast across the plains by Thursday morning. The greatest coverage of precipitation is expected Wednesday evening as the core of the wave passes over. Snow levels will hover around 8,500-9,000ft through Wednesday, and lower to around 6,000-,6500ft by Thursday morning. Snow can be expected above these levels, with snow favoring the higher terrain. The heaviest snow can be expected across the central mountains, with 4-10 inches of snowfall. Other ranges can expect around 1-4 inches of snow. Rain showers can be expected below these levels, primarily for the plains and valleys. With that said, as snow levels drop Wednesday night into Thursday morning, light snow may develop across the Palmer Divide. With that all said, showers are anticipated to start dissipating by early Thursday morning, with dry conditions then prevailing Thursday afternoon. Beyond all of that, mostly clear skies early Wednesday will become cloudy through Wednesday afternoon and night, with clear skies then returning through Thursday as the wave pushes east. Winds can also be expected to remain relatively light, with winds around 10-15 mph, and occasional gusts to around 20-25 mph. Looking at temperatures, cool and near seasonable temperatures can be expected across the region, with a slight dip in temperatures Thursday as a cold front is dragged southward late Wednesday with the wave passage.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Friday - Saturday: For the end of the week and into the start of the weekend, some active weather may persist for south central and southeastern Colorado. Another wave is expected to push across the region through this timeframe, but there is some uncertainty in how the wave will evolve, primarily in will it be a more open wave or more compact wave like the Wednesday-Thursday one. As of now, current leaning is more open, which ensemble guidance supports, leading to higher confidence in that pattern progression. With this pattern, a brief uptick in ascent can be expected, which may help support isolated to widely scattered shower development across the region. The greatest coverage of showers can be anticipated along the mountains, where any forcing will be maximized. With that all said, any showers present would be expected to dissipate through Saturday, as the wave drops to the south/east and forcing lessens. Otherwise, partly to mostly cloudy skies can be expected, with winds remaining relatively light around 10-15 mph. As for temperatures, they will also remain fairly stable, with much of the area hovering around to slightly above seasonal values.

Sunday - Tuesday: For the end of the weekend and into early next week. Quiet weather makes a return to south central and southeastern Colorado. Overall, ridging is expected to make a return, bringing increased subsidence and drier air to the area. Given this, dry conditions are anticipated through this period. With that said, there are signals of another wave passage through Tuesday, but confidence in that feature impacting the area is very low (10-20%) at this time. Otherwise, mostly clear to partly cloudy skies and light winds can be anticipated. Temperatures through this period will also start a warming trend, with much of south central and southeastern Colorado warming to above seasonal values.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Uncertainty in the forecast increases quite a bit for next week. With the ridge not expected to stick around, there is potential for storm systems to move onshore and bring impacts to the forecast area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A weak system traverses the Great Basin on Wednesday bringing light valley rain and high elevation snowfall to northern and central Utah.
- A second weak storm system may graze northern Utah on Friday before high pressure builds for the weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Weak high pressure has shifted east of the area this evening as a Pacific storm system moves into the Great Basin. Clouds are already streaming into the area and will increase overnight. The system is expected to track across Utah and southwest Wyoming during the day tomorrow, dropping temperatures to up to 10F below seasonal normals and bringing some generally light showers to primarily northern and central Utah. The limiting factors for precip will be the progressive nature of the system as well as the lack of moisture associated with the system, particularly compared to the systems that have been impacting the area as of late.

Weak ridging is expected to move back over the area for Thursday, but guidance is indicating that a weak grazing shortwave will act to temporarily flatten the ridge and perhaps bring a few showers near the Utah/Idaho border. As that wave moves through, guidance is becoming increasingly confident that a ridge will develop off the Pacific coast before moving across Utah and southwest Wyoming for the weekend. This will bring dry conditions and a steady warming trend in temperatures, with maxes expected to move above seasonal normals by Sunday afternoon.

Uncertainty in the forecast increases quite a bit for next week. With the ridge not expected to stick around, there is potential for storm systems to move onshore and bring impacts to the forecast area. However, there is quite a bit of spread in the guidance with regard to the details of any particular system, with some models showing high pressure returning for the middle to latter part of next week.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: On high-elevation alpine slopes, you can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you.

The most dangerous slopes face northwest to northeast through east, where winds drifted snow onto lee slopes, forming thicker, more connected slabs. Below about 12,000 feet, avalanches will become smaller and more isolated.
You can find safer travel options at lower elevations and in wind-sheltered areas.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. Steer around steep slopes near ridgelines with continuous, firm snow cover. You might find these slopes to avoid at high elevations.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
Seasonal SNOW AND PRECIPITATION Comparison
(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

• December - 68" (12.6" SWE)
• January - 37" (5.1" SWE)
• February - 41" (5.4" SWE)
• March - 24" (5.2" SWE) Peak Height of Snow - 70" (03/05)

2735.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. You could trigger an avalanche on high-elevation north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, if you find firm, hollow snow, Just steer around these drifts of snow to avoid potential problems.
